passages.t: Shepherds who feed themselves, and the Shepherd who seeks
passages.happening:
“Woe to the shepherds of Israel, who only feed themselves! Should not the shepherds feed their flock?” (verse 2). ‘You eat the fat, wear the wool, and butcher the fattened sheep, but you do not feed the flock’ (verse 3). ‘You have not strengthened the weak, healed the sick, bound up the injured, brought back the strays, or searched for the lost. Instead, you have ruled them with violence and cruelty’ (verse 4). So the sheep were scattered and became food for wild beasts (verses 5-6). God is against the shepherds, and he will rescue his flock from their mouths (verses 7-10).

‘Behold, I Myself will search for My flock and seek them out’ (verse 11). He will gather them from every place they were scattered ‘on a day of clouds and darkness’ (verse 12), bring them home and feed them on the mountains of Israel (verses 13-14). ‘I will seek the lost, bring back the strays, bind up the broken, and strengthen the weak’ (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
Calling a king a shepherd was common across the ancient Near East; Hammurabi used the title in the prologue to his laws. The picture meant care as well as rule. A good shepherd leads the flock to pasture and water, protects it from predators, carries the injured and goes after strays. David himself had been a shepherd boy.

The shepherds here are Israel's kings and ruling classes, above all Judah's last kings and their officials, whose policies ended in Jerusalem's destruction and the scattering of the people. A shepherd was entitled to some milk, wool and meat, but these took the best and left the flock to die.
passages.later: Jeremiah said, “Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of My pasture!” (Jeremiah 23:1). The psalm begins, ‘The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want’ (Psalm 23:1).
passages.asks: God's complaint was that the shepherds fed themselves. Ask whom you are responsible to care for, at home, at work or in church. And ask whether you are feeding them or feeding yourself.

passages.t: One shepherd, and a covenant of peace
passages.happening:
God will also judge between sheep and sheep. The strong have pushed the weak aside with shoulder and horn, eaten the best pasture and trampled the rest, drunk clear water and muddied what was left (verses 17-21). God will save his flock and judge between them (verse 22).

‘I will appoint over them one shepherd, My servant David, and he will feed them. He will feed them and be their shepherd’ (verse 23). ‘I, the LORD, will be their God, and My servant David will be a prince among them’ (verse 24). ‘I will make with them a covenant of peace’ (verse 25). Wild beasts will be gone, rain will fall in season, the trees will bear fruit, and they will live securely with no one to make them afraid (verses 25-28). ‘You are My flock, the sheep of My pasture, My people, and I am your God’ (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
Verses 17 to 22 add a scene any herder knew: strong rams and goats shoving the weaker animals aside, trampling pasture and muddying water they had already used. The problem was not only the rulers but the powerful within the flock.

The promise of a new David came when no son of David ruled anywhere. Jehoiachin was a prisoner in Babylon, and the line seemed at an end. The hope reaches beyond anything the exiles could see.
passages.later: Jeremiah promised that Israel would serve ‘David their king, whom I will raise up for them’ (Jeremiah 30:9). Hosea said the same (Hosea 3:5).
passages.hard:
Does the promise of God's servant David mean that David himself will return?

Almost all interpreters, Jewish and Christian, take David as a name for a king from David's line, as a dynasty can be called by its founder's name, not David raised from the dead. Hosea and Jeremiah use the name the same way. Jewish tradition has read the promise of the Messiah, the anointed king of David's line. Christians see it fulfilled in Jesus, born of David's line, and have read his words, ‘I am the good shepherd’ (John 10:11), against this chapter; the Gospel does not quote Ezekiel there, so that is a reading. Some scholars read the promise more narrowly, of the hope for a restored prince of David's line after the exile, a hope that Zerubbabel briefly seemed to raise.

These readings need not exclude each other. The chapter's hope reaches past any ruler of the return, since it describes one shepherd over a reunited people in a covenant of lasting peace.
passages.asks: God promised to judge between strong sheep and weak. Ask whether you have used your strength to push others aside. And ask what it means to belong to the Shepherd who strengthens the weak.
